chapters.title: Fullness and Fulfil
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, to fulfil is to fill something full: a jar, a span of time, a promise, a life
chapters.trueMeaning: Filled to the brim, brought to completeness
chapters.nutshell: We usually hear “fulfil” as “a prediction came true”. The Hebrew *male* and the Greek *plēroō* first mean **to fill**: a jar is filled, time fills up, a word is filled out in action. When Jesus “fulfils” the Torah and the prophets, he fills them to the brim with their full meaning and lives them out completely.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical fulfilment is not ticking a box but filling something full, and God's goal is a world, a people and a life filled with his presence.
skeleton: We usually hear “fulfil” as a prediction that came true
Male: to be full, to fill; time fills up like a jar
Melo and shalem: the fullness of the earth and wholeness
The Septuagint chose plērōma and plēroō, words for a full basket or a full crew
Translators use many English words, so the picture of filling is hidden
Jesus fills the Torah full, and love fills up the law
In Christ the whole fullness of God lives in a body, against later Gnostic ideas
We are invited to be filled and to fill God's word out in our lives

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: When most of us read “this was to fulfil what the prophet said”, we picture a prediction and an event that matched it, like a box being ticked. Fulfilment sounds like a finished checklist: the prophecy came true, so we can move on. And “fullness” sounds like a vague, mystical word we sing but rarely explain.

The old English word *fulfil* actually comes from “fill” and “full”: to fill something full. The Hebrew and Greek words behind it carry the same everyday picture. A jar is filled, a season comes to its full time, a promise is filled out in action, a person is filled with the Spirit. Keeping that picture in mind changes how we read many famous verses.

sections.h: Male: to be full and to fill
p: The Hebrew verb *male* (מָלֵא) means **to be full** and, in another form, **to fill**. God blesses the creatures: “Be fruitful and multiply and **fill** the waters” and tells the first humans to “fill the earth” (Genesis 1:22, 28). Barns are “filled with plenty” (Proverbs 3:10). It is a word of jars, storehouses and a world teeming with life.

Hebrew also speaks of **time** filling up like a vessel. After seven years of work Jacob says to Laban, “Give me my wife, for **my days are full**” (Genesis 29:21, literally). A mother waits “until the days of her purifying are full” (Leviticus 12:4). A set period has a measure, and when the last day is poured in, it is complete.

The same verb is used when a **word** is carried out. Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood, “thus **fulfilling** the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli” (1 Kings 2:27). At the Temple's dedication Solomon praises God, who spoke with his mouth “and with his hand has **fulfilled** it” (1 Kings 8:15, 24). A promise is like an empty outline; God's action fills it in.

One more picture: to ordain a priest, Hebrew says to **“fill his hand”** (*millē yad*, מִלֵּא יָד: Exodus 28:41; 29:9). Many scholars think this comes from placing portions of the offering into the priest's hands (Exodus 29:24), though the origin is debated. Either way, to be set apart for service was to have your hands filled.

sections.h: Melo and shalem: fullness and wholeness
p: From *male* comes the noun *melo* (מְלֹא), **fullness**: everything that fills a space. “The earth is the LORD's and **the fullness thereof**” (Psalm 24:1): not only the ground but every animal, plant and person on it. The seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; **the whole earth is full of his glory**” (Isaiah 6:3), or more literally, “**the fullness of all the earth is his glory**”. Jews still say these words every day in the *Kedushah* of the Amidah prayer.

When Jacob blesses Ephraim, he says his offspring will become *melo ha-goyim* (מְלֹא הַגּוֹיִם), literally “the fullness of the nations” (Genesis 48:19). Many scholars hear an echo of this phrase when Paul speaks of Israel's hardening “until **the fullness of the Gentiles** has come in” (Romans 11:25).

A neighbour word is *shalem* (שָׁלֵם), **whole, complete**, from the same root family as *shalom*. God tells Abraham his descendants must wait, “for the iniquity of the Amorites is **not yet complete**” (Genesis 15:16): their measure was not yet full. And Solomon prays, “Let your heart be **wholly true** to the LORD our God” (1 Kings 8:61; KJV “perfect”). Fullness in Hebrew is not only quantity but **wholeness**, nothing missing.

sections.h: The Greek words and the Septuagint link
p: When Jewish scholars translated the Scriptures into Greek, they chose *plēroō* (πληρόω), “to fill”, and *plērōma* (πλήρωμα), “that which fills, fullness”. The Greek of Psalm 24:1, “the earth is the Lord's and **its plērōma**”, is quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:26. So the New Testament's fullness words come to us already filled with Hebrew meaning.

In everyday Greek, *plērōma* was a down-to-earth word. In Mark it is the **patch** that fills a hole in a garment (Mark 2:21) and the **basketfuls** of leftover bread (Mark 6:43; 8:20). In ordinary Greek it could mean the full crew of a ship. The adjective *plērēs* (πλήρης) means “full”: the Word was “**full of grace and truth**” (John 1:14), an echo of God “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

Time fills up in Greek too. Jesus begins his preaching, “**The time is fulfilled**, and the kingdom of God is at hand” (Mark 1:15), and Paul says, “When **the fullness of time** had come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4). The jar of history had reached the brim.

Two other verbs mean to complete or bring to the goal: *teleō* (τελέω) and *teleioō* (τελειόω). On the cross, “knowing that all was now **finished**, that the Scripture might be **fulfilled**”, Jesus said, “**It is finished**” (*tetelestai*, τετέλεσται: John 19:28, 30). *Teleō* was also the ordinary word for paying a tax (Matthew 17:24; Romans 13:6), so some hear “paid in full” in Jesus' cry. In John the main stress is the **work completed** (John 17:4).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: Because one Hebrew or Greek verb covers jars, time, promises and people, English translators must choose different words in different places. That is usually wise: no single English word fits every context. But the reader loses the thread that ties these verses together.

Genesis 29:21 is “my days are fulfilled” in the KJV, but modern versions often say “my time is completed” (ESV). Exodus 28:41 says “consecrate them” (KJV), because “fill their hand” makes no sense in English, yet the picture of filled hands disappears. Isaiah 6:3 is smoothed to “the whole earth is full of his glory”, hiding the bolder Hebrew “the fullness of the earth is his glory”.

In the New Testament, the same verb *plēroō* becomes “fulfil the word of God” (Colossians 1:25, KJV) but “make the word of God fully known” (ESV), and “I have fully preached the gospel” (Romans 15:19, KJV). The translators are explaining what Paul meant, which helps, but the link with Jesus “fulfilling” the Scriptures is no longer visible.

> The biggest loss is in our minds, not on the page: we have learned to hear “fulfil” only as “a prediction came true”. Matthew can say Jesus' return from Egypt “fulfilled” Hosea 11:1, a verse about Israel's exodus that predicted nothing (Matthew 2:15). He means Jesus **filled Israel's story full** by living it again.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In ancient Israel, fullness was a farmer's and a householder's word. Harvests were measured in jars and baskets; a good year meant full barns and overflowing vats (Proverbs 3:10; Joel 2:24). Life was ordered by fixed spans of time: seven days, the days of purification, seven years of service, the Sabbath year and the Jubilee. A promise or a vow had a measure, and people waited for it to be filled.

At the centre was the sanctuary. When the Tabernacle was finished, “the glory of the LORD **filled** the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34), and the same happened at Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). For a Jew, the deepest fullness was **God's presence filling the place he chose**.

In the Greco-Roman world, *plērōma* belonged to trade and travel: a ship's full crew and cargo, a full measure of grain, the patch that makes a garment whole. Later, in the second century, some Gnostic teachers (as the church father Irenaeus describes) used *Plērōma* for a spiritual realm of divine beings far above the material world. That is a very different idea from the Bible's earthy fullness.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: filling the Torah full
p: Jesus says, “Do not think that I have come to **abolish** the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to **fulfil** them” (Matthew 5:17). The Greek pair is *katalyō* (καταλύω), “loosen, tear down”, and *plēroō*, “fill”. Scholars compare this to later rabbinic debate language, where to “establish” (*qiyyem*, קִיֵּם) the Torah meant to interpret and live it rightly, and to “cancel” (*bittel*, בִּטֵּל) meant to empty it by wrong teaching.

Read this way, Jesus is not ending the Torah. He is **filling it to the brim**: teaching its full intent (“you have heard… but I say to you”, Matthew 5:21–48) and living it completely. Paul uses similar language: “Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we **uphold** the law” (Romans 3:31).

Paul also says that love **fills up** the law: “The one who loves another has fulfilled the law… love is the **fulfilling** of the law” (Romans 13:8, 10; compare Galatians 5:14). Literally, love is the law's *plērōma*, the thing that fills it full. “Bear one another's burdens, and so **fulfil** the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

sections.h: All the fullness in a human body
p: Paul's letters to the Colossians and Ephesians use *plērōma* in their highest sense. “In him all the **fullness** of God was pleased to dwell” (Colossians 1:19), and “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells **bodily**” (Colossians 2:9). As God's glory once filled the Tabernacle, now God's fullness fills a human life, flesh and blood.

That is the opposite of the later Gnostic picture, where the divine fullness stays far away from matter and bodies. Some scholars think Colossians already answers early ideas of that kind; whatever the background, Paul's point is plain: you do not need to climb past the body or past Christ to reach God. **“You have been filled in him”** (Colossians 2:10).

And the fullness overflows into his people. The church is “his body, **the fullness of him who fills all in all**” (Ephesians 1:23). Paul prays that believers may “be filled with all the fullness of God” (Ephesians 3:19) and grow “to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13). From his fullness “we have all received, grace upon grace” (John 1:16).

sections.h: Living it out
p: If fulfilment means filling full, then God's purpose is not to empty the world but to fill it: with life, with justice, with his glory. Our faith is not a box of predictions ticked off, but a story God is filling to the brim. You are part of that story.

Paul says, “**Be filled** with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18), and the result he describes is ordinary: singing together, giving thanks, and treating one another well at home and at work. To be filled is to make room for God in daily life. Like a priest whose hands are filled, you are given something to carry and to serve with.

Finally, the Bible's sense of time invites patience. Some promises are still filling up, like Jacob's seven years that “seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had” (Genesis 29:20). God is not late. When the measure is full, he acts, as he did “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4).

chapters.title: Love
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, love is loyal, it acts, and it comes from the gut as much as from the heart
chapters.trueMeaning: Loyal, faithful, acting love; tender compassion
chapters.nutshell: In English “love” is mostly a feeling. The Hebrew Bible speaks of *ahavah*, love that chooses and acts; *chesed*, faithful covenant love; and *rachamim*, tender compassion from the word for “womb”. The Septuagint chose the Greek *agapaō* for this Hebrew love, and the New Testament fills it with the life and death of Jesus.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical love is not first a feeling but loyal, tender, practical faithfulness, the way God loves Israel and the way we are called to love God and neighbour.
skeleton: We usually think of love as a feeling, and hear that agape is a special “God kind” of love

Chesed: covenant loyal-love that keeps faith
Rachamim: womb-love, compassion; dod: the beloved
The Septuagint chose agapaō, so agapē gets its meaning from the Hebrew and from context

Love is loyalty in action, tender toward the weak, and it fills up the law

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: In English we “love” pizza, a football team, our children and God, all with one word. Usually we mean a **feeling**: warmth, attraction, liking. Feelings come and go, so love can seem to come and go too. Many people think love cannot be commanded, because you cannot order someone to feel something.

In church we often hear another idea: that Greek had four words for love, and that *agapē* was a special, unconditional “God kind” of love. There is some truth in it, but it is simpler and richer to start where Jesus and the apostles started: with the **Hebrew Bible**, where love is loyal, active and deeply tender.

sections.h: Ahav and ahavah: love that chooses and acts
p: The main Hebrew verb is *ahav* (אָהַב), “to love”, and the noun is *ahavah* (אַהֲבָה). Its first appearance in the Bible is a father's love: “Take your son, your only son Isaac, **whom you love**” (Genesis 22:2). It is used of a husband's love: Jacob served seven years for Rachel, “and they seemed to him but a few days because of the **love** he had for her” (Genesis 29:20).

Yet the Torah also **commands** love: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5), and “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), even the foreigner: “You shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 19:34). A feeling cannot be ordered, but **loyalty and care** can. In the next verses of the Shema, love means keeping God's words, teaching them and living by them (Deuteronomy 6:6–9).

God's own love is a **choice**: “It was not because you were more in number… that the LORD set his love on you… but it is because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Love in Hebrew is not earned, and it is not just emotion. It is a faithful decision that shows itself in action.

sections.h: Chesed: covenant loyal-love
p: The richest Hebrew love word may be *chesed* (חֶסֶד). It means **loyal love, steadfast kindness, faithfulness inside a relationship**. When God reveals his name to Moses he is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and **abounding in chesed and faithfulness**” (Exodus 34:6). Psalm 136 repeats twenty-six times, “for his *chesed* endures forever”.

*Chesed* is love that keeps its promises, especially when the other person has no claim and cannot repay. Ruth stays loyal to her widowed mother-in-law, and Boaz praises her *chesed* (Ruth 3:10). Micah sums up what God requires: “to do justice, and to **love chesed**, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).

God says through Hosea, “For I desire **chesed** and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). Jesus quotes this verse twice when religious people object to his mercy toward sinners and his disciples (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).

sections.h: Rachamim and dod: womb-love and the beloved
p: The word *rachamim* (רַחֲמִים), **compassion, tender mercy**, comes from the same root as *rechem* (רֶחֶם), “womb”. It is the love a mother feels for the child she carried. When King Solomon threatened to divide the baby, the true mother cried out “because **her compassion grew warm** for her son” (1 Kings 3:26, literally). God says, “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no **compassion** on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15).

Fathers have it too: “As a father **shows compassion** to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13). In Jewish prayer God is often called *HaRachaman*, “the Compassionate One”, for example in the blessings after meals.

Then there is *dod* (דּוֹד), “**beloved**”, the word of the Song of Songs: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2:16); “I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine” (Song 6:3). The Song says that “love is strong as death… many waters cannot quench love” (Song 8:6–7). Jewish tradition read it as a picture of God and Israel, and Rabbi Akiva called it the “Holy of Holies” of Scripture (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5). The name *David* (דָּוִד) is probably related to this word.

sections.h: The Greek words and the Septuagint's choice
p: When Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek, they used *agapaō* (ἀγαπάω) for nearly every *ahav*. The noun *agapē* (ἀγάπη) was a rare word in Greek before this; the Septuagint made it common. So *agapē* did not arrive with a ready-made meaning of “divine love”. It got its meaning from the **Hebrew love** it translated, and then from Jesus.

In fact *agapaō* can describe bad love. In the Greek of 2 Samuel 13:15, Amnon's twisted desire for Tamar is called *agapē*. Jesus says people “**loved** the darkness rather than the light” (John 3:19), and Paul writes that Demas, “**in love** with this present world”, deserted him (2 Timothy 4:10). The word itself is not magic. What makes NT *agapē* special is **who loves and how**: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

*Phileō* (φιλέω) is the love of friends and family, and can mean “to kiss” (Mark 14:44). A *philos* (φίλος) is a friend: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his **friends**” (John 15:13). *Storgē*, family affection, appears in compounds: people “without natural affection” (*astorgos*, Romans 1:31, KJV) and “be kindly affectioned one to another” (*philostorgos*, Romans 12:10, KJV). *Erōs*, passionate desire, is **never used in the New Testament**.

Finally, *splanchnizomai* (σπλαγχνίζομαι) means “to be moved in the gut”, from *splanchna*, “inner parts”. The father saw his lost son “and **felt compassion**, and ran and embraced him” (Luke 15:20); so did the Samaritan (Luke 10:33). It is the Greek match for Hebrew *rachamim*: love felt deep inside, that moves you to act.

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: No English word covers *chesed*, so every version struggles. The KJV uses “mercy”, “kindness”, “goodness” and “lovingkindness” (a word going back to the sixteenth-century translator Miles Coverdale). The ESV and NRSV often say “**steadfast love**”, and the NIV “love” or “unfailing love”. So Psalm 136 is “his mercy endureth for ever” (KJV), “his steadfast love endures forever” (ESV) and “His love endures forever” (NIV). Each catches part of it; none catches the **loyalty** and the covenant together.

Hosea 6:6 shows the chain from Hebrew to Greek to English. The Septuagint rendered *chesed* there with *eleos* (ἔλεος), “mercy”, and Matthew quotes the Greek: “I desire **mercy**, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13). So English readers hear “mercy”, while Hosea meant loyal covenant love as well.

In 1 Corinthians 13 the KJV says “**charity**”: “faith, hope, charity… but the greatest of these is charity.” It followed the Latin Vulgate's *caritas*, which meant dear, precious love. Tyndale had used “love”. Today “charity” means giving to the poor, so the KJV's word now misleads, and modern versions rightly say “love”.

In John 21:15–17 Jesus asks twice with *agapaō* and once with *phileō*, and Peter always answers with *phileō*. Most English versions use “love” every time, because English has one verb. Scholars debate how much the switch means: John uses both verbs for the Father loving the Son (John 3:35; 5:20), and the conversation was likely in Aramaic. The clear point is Jesus' **threefold restoring** of Peter after his threefold denial.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In ancient Israel love lived inside **covenant and family**. Marriage, kinship and hospitality were duties of loyalty, not only emotions. A kinsman-redeemer like Boaz showed love by buying back land and marrying a widow (Ruth 4). Ancient treaties from Israel's neighbours asked subject kings to “love” the great king, meaning to be loyal; scholars widely see this background in Deuteronomy. Even King Hiram of Tyre “always **loved** David” (1 Kings 5:1), that is, he was his faithful ally.

Because love meant loyalty, “hate” could mean to reject or not choose (see the study on *sane*). Love was shown in **deeds**: bread for the poor, gleanings left for the widow and the stranger (Leviticus 19:9–10), honest weights, care for the weak.

In the Greco-Roman world, *philia* (friendship) was a central virtue. Philosophers wrote long books on it, and a famous proverb said “friends have all things in common”. Luke may echo this when he says the believers “had **everything in common**” (Acts 4:32). Love in that world often worked through patronage, gifts and returning favours. Jesus overturns that: “If you love those who love you, what reward do you have?… Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44–46).

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: love in a Jewish key
p: Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus joins two verses from the Torah: the Shema, “love the Lord your God…” (Deuteronomy 6:5), and “love your neighbour as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). “On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:37–40). Jewish teachers also saw love at the centre. Hillel taught, “What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow: that is the whole Torah” (Talmud Shabbat 31a), and Rabbi Akiva called Leviticus 19:18 “a great principle of the Torah” (Sifra).

Jesus widens “neighbour” to include the enemy and the outsider, as in the parable of the Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37). He gives a “new commandment”: “love one another: **just as I have loved you**” (John 13:34). The measure of love is now his own self-giving.

The apostles describe love as **action**: “Love is patient and kind… it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). John says, “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and then: “let us not love in word or talk but **in deed and in truth**” (1 John 3:18). That is Hebrew *chesed* in Greek clothes.

sections.h: Living it out
p: If love is loyalty in action, you do not have to wait for a feeling before you love. You can choose to keep faith with your spouse, your friend, your church and your neighbour, and often the feelings follow. When love feels weak, ask: “What would *chesed* do here?”

Biblical love is also **tender**. *Rachamim* and *splanchna* remind us that God's love is felt in the gut, like a mother's love. We are invited to let our hearts be moved by people in need, as Jesus was moved by the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36), and then to act.

> “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). The world is meant to recognise Jesus' followers not by their arguments, but by their loyal, tender, practical love.

chapters.title: Glory
chapters.subtitle: In Hebrew, glory is weight: what is heavy, substantial and worthy of honour
chapters.trueMeaning: Weight, worth, honour, God's presence revealed
chapters.nutshell: We picture glory as bright light or fame. The Hebrew *kavod* comes from a word for **heavy**: glory is weight, substance, worth. To “honour” your parents is to give them weight. The Septuagint chose the Greek *doxa*, which first meant “opinion” or “reputation”, and filled it with the Hebrew sense of God's weighty, shining presence.
chapters.bigIdea: God's glory is the weight of who he really is, made visible among his people, and to glorify him is to give him the weight he deserves.
skeleton: We usually picture glory as shining light, fame or praise words
Kavod comes from kaved, “heavy”: weight, wealth, importance
To honour is to give weight; to despise is to treat as light
God's glory comes to dwell: Sinai, Tabernacle, Temple, and the later word Shekhinah
Greek doxa meant “opinion, reputation” until the Septuagint made it “glory”
Translators use glory, honour, wealth and praise, and the weight picture is lost
Jesus reveals glory on the cross, against an honour-seeking world
We glorify God by giving him weight in all of life, and we are changed into his glory

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: When we hear “glory”, we usually think of **bright light**: a halo, a shining cloud, golden rays in a painting. Or we think of fame: a sports star's moment of glory. In church, “giving glory to God” can sound like saying the right praise words in a song.

The Hebrew Bible starts somewhere more solid. Its main word for glory, *kavod*, is related to the word for **heavy**. Glory is **weight**: what is substantial, valuable and worthy of honour. Light often comes with God's glory, but the core idea is that God is the most real, weighty and important being there is.

sections.h: Kavod: the weight of a person
p: The verb *kaved* (כָּבֵד) means **to be heavy**, and the noun *kavod* (כָּבוֹד) means **weight, wealth, honour, glory**. Abram was “very **heavy** in livestock, in silver and in gold” (Genesis 13:2, literally); our versions say “very rich”. When Laban's sons complained about Jacob, they said, “From what was our father's he has gained all this ***kavod***” (Genesis 31:1), meaning his wealth.

A person's *kavod* is his weight in society: his wealth, position and reputation. Joseph tells his brothers, “You must tell my father of all my **honour** in Egypt” (Genesis 45:13). In Hebrew thinking, someone with *kavod* is a person who counts, whose word carries weight.

The Bible even plays on the word. Old Eli the priest fell and died, “for he was an old man and **heavy**” (1 Samuel 4:18, *kaved*). On the same day his daughter-in-law named her baby *Ichabod* (אִי־כָבוֹד), “no glory”, saying, “**The glory has departed from Israel**, for the ark of God has been captured” (1 Samuel 4:21). The heavy priest fell, and Israel's true weight, God's presence, was gone.

sections.h: Giving weight: honour, shame and a heavy heart
p: The same root gives the command, “**Honour** your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12), literally “make them heavy”: give them weight in your life. Honour is not only a feeling of respect; it is shown in how you speak to them, care for them and take their words seriously. God says through Malachi, “If I am a father, where is my **honour**?” (Malachi 1:6).

The opposite of heavy is **light**. God tells Eli, “Those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me shall be **lightly esteemed**” (1 Samuel 2:30). “Honour” is *kaved*; “lightly esteemed” is *qalal* (קָלַל), “to be light”. To despise someone is to treat them as a lightweight.

The root also describes Pharaoh. Again and again his heart is “hardened”, but often the Hebrew says it was **heavy**: “Pharaoh's heart is **heavy**; he refuses to let the people go” (Exodus 7:14; compare 8:15; 9:34). Pharaoh made his own heart heavy and would not give the LORD any weight, so God said, “**I will get glory** over Pharaoh” (Exodus 14:4), the same root again. In the end, God's weight is shown.

sections.h: The glory that comes to dwell
p: Moses asks, “Please show me your **glory**” (Exodus 33:18). God answers, “I will make all my **goodness** pass before you and will proclaim before you my name” (33:19). God's glory is not only a sight; it is his character: merciful, gracious and faithful (34:6).

Then the glory comes to live among the people. “The glory of the LORD **dwelt** on Mount Sinai” (Exodus 24:16). When the Tabernacle was finished, “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD **filled** the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34), and later Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). Ezekiel sees the glory leave the Temple before its destruction (Ezekiel 10:18) and, in a vision, return (Ezekiel 43:2–5).

Later rabbinic Judaism used the word *Shekhinah* (שְׁכִינָה), from *shakhan* “to dwell”, for **God's dwelling presence**. It is not a Bible word, but it grew from these texts. The Mishnah says that when ten sit together and study Torah, “the Shekhinah rests among them” (Mishnah Avot 3:6), which many compare to Jesus' words in Matthew 18:20.

Other Hebrew words add colour: *tif'eret* (תִּפְאֶרֶת), **beauty, splendour**, and *hod* (הוֹד), **majesty**. The priest's garments were made “for glory and for **beauty**” (Exodus 28:2). David blesses God: “Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the **glory** and the victory and the **majesty**” (1 Chronicles 29:11), words that many see behind the later ending of the Lord's Prayer, “for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory”.

sections.h: Doxa: from opinion to glory
p: In ordinary Greek, *doxa* (δόξα) came from *dokeō*, “to think, to seem”. It meant **opinion, expectation, reputation**: what people think of you. We still have it in “orthodoxy”, “right opinion”. When the Septuagint translators needed a word for *kavod*, they chose *doxa*, probably because *kavod* also means honour and reputation. Over time, through the Bible, *doxa* came to mean the **radiant presence and worth of God**.

John writes, “The Word became flesh and **dwelt** among us, and we have seen his **glory**, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The verb “dwelt” is *skēnoō*, “to pitch a tent”, recalling the Tabernacle that the glory filled. At Cana Jesus “manifested his glory” (John 2:11), and he prays, “Glorify me… with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5).

Paul, a Hebrew speaker writing Greek, keeps the weight picture: “this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal **weight of glory**” (2 Corinthians 4:17). The verb *doxazō* (δοξάζω), “to glorify”, means to show or give honour: “let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and **give glory** to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: Because *kavod* covers wealth, honour, importance and God's shining presence, translators rightly choose different English words: “glory”, “honour”, “riches”, “wealth”. In Genesis 31:1 the KJV says Jacob “hath gotten all this **glory**”, while the ESV says “all this **wealth**”. Both are correct; but the reader cannot see that Jacob's flocks and God's glory are described with the same word.

In Exodus, most versions say Pharaoh's heart was “hardened”, because that is what a heavy, unmoving heart means in English. But Hebrew uses three different verbs for Pharaoh's heart, and the “heavy” one links directly to God “getting glory” (Exodus 14:4). The wordplay disappears.

Psalm 16:9 says, literally, “my heart is glad and **my glory** rejoices”. The KJV keeps “my glory”; the ESV says “my whole being”, because *kavod* here seems to mean one's inner self or honour. The Septuagint read it as “my tongue”, and Peter quotes that Greek (Acts 2:26), so some versions such as the NIV say “tongue”.

In John 12:43, the KJV says people “loved the **praise** of men more than the praise of God”, while the ESV says “the **glory** that comes from man”. *Doxa* here means reputation, and the KJV chose the sense that fits. But it hides how John contrasts human glory with the glory of God revealed in Jesus throughout his Gospel.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In ancient Israel, wealth was literally weighed. Silver was weighed out on scales, and the word *shekel* comes from *shaqal*, “to weigh” (Genesis 23:16). A heavy man was a rich man, and a heavy name was an honoured one. Society ran on **honour and shame**: elders at the city gate, parents in the home, and the king at court were all to be given weight. To shame someone was to make them light.

For Israel, the highest *kavod* belonged to the God who chose to live among them, first in a tent and then in the Temple. In synagogue prayer the *Kedushah* still joins Isaiah 6:3, “the whole earth is full of his glory”, with Ezekiel 3:12, “Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place.”

In the Greco-Roman world, *doxa* was **public reputation**. Cities set up inscriptions honouring benefactors; generals celebrated triumphs; emperors were praised for their glory. Men competed for honour. Jesus speaks straight into that world: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (John 5:44). Paul warns against *kenodoxia* (κενοδοξία), “empty glory”, KJV “vainglory” (Philippians 2:3).

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: glory in a crucified Messiah
p: In John's Gospel the great hour of glory is the **cross**. “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be **glorified**. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:23–24). “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” John adds, “He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die” (12:32–33).

This turns the honour world upside down. The one who has the greatest weight of all lays aside his status and takes “the form of a servant… becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross”. Therefore God exalted him, so that every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, “**to the glory of God the Father**” (Philippians 2:7–11). Paul can even say the rulers “crucified the **Lord of glory**” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

And the glory is shared. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), but now “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image **from one degree of glory to another**” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The glory that once filled the Tabernacle now shines in transformed lives: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27).

sections.h: Living it out
p: To glorify God is to **give him weight**: to take him seriously in your decisions, your money, your time and your relationships. It is more than singing; it is letting God be the heaviest reality in your life. “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

It also means giving proper weight to others: honouring parents, elders and the people society treats as lightweights. And it means not chasing empty glory, the approval of others, which is as light as air. Jesus' followers are free from that race, because the only weight that finally counts is the honour that comes from God.

> The Bible ends with a city that needs no sun, “for the **glory of God** gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). The story moves toward a world filled with God's weighty, shining presence, and you are being prepared for it, “from one degree of glory to another”.

Who around you is treated as a “lightweight”? How could you give them honour this week?

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew root of kavod (glory) basically mean?
quiz.why: Kavod comes from kaved, “to be heavy”: glory is weight and worth.

quiz.q: In 1 Samuel 2:30, what is the opposite of “honour” (kaved)?
quiz.why: God says those who despise him will be “lightly esteemed”: heavy versus light.

quiz.q: What did the Greek word doxa mean before the Septuagint?
quiz.why: Doxa came from dokeō, “to think, seem”; the Septuagint used it for kavod, and it came to mean glory.

quiz.q: Where is the word Shekhinah found?
options: In later rabbinic writings, not in the Bible
quiz.why: Shekhinah is a later Jewish term for God's dwelling presence, built on biblical ideas.

quiz.q: In John's Gospel, where is Jesus' great hour of glory?
quiz.why: Jesus speaks of being glorified and “lifted up”, showing the kind of death he would die (John 12:23, 32–33).

terms.def: Hebrew glory: weight, wealth, honour, and God's presence made known.
Hebrew “to be heavy”; also “to honour” (Exodus 20:12).
“No glory”: the name given when the ark was captured (1 Samuel 4:21).
Later Jewish word for God's dwelling presence, from shakhan, “to dwell”.
Greek “opinion, reputation”, which through the Septuagint came to mean God's glory.
Greek “empty glory”, seeking reputation for its own sake (Philippians 2:3).
Part of Jewish prayer joining Isaiah 6:3 and Ezekiel 3:12 in praise of God's glory.
